items.title: Multi-repository support and other improvements for GitHub in Slack and Teams
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: @GitHub in Slack and Teams now supports working across multiple repositories in a single conversation. Whether you’re creating issues, opening pull requests, or investigating bugs, you can work across repositories without switching conversations. For example, you can ask @GitHub to: Create issues from conversations: “@GitHub Create an issue in github/issues to track this bug, using the context from this thread.” Make code changes: “@GitHub Fix this bug in our frontend repository and open a PR with the changes.” Track your PRs: “@GitHub Show me all my open PRs across repositories and highlight which ones need my attention.” Investigate bugs: “@GitHub Investigate this issue using the code in our frontend and backend repositories.” You can do all of this directly from Slack or Teams, without switching repositories or starting a new conversation. Additional improvements We’ve also made several improvements to GitHub in Slack and Microsoft Teams: More natural conversations: Mention @GitHub anywhere in your message, not just at the beginning. Smoother repository switching: Move between repositories more easily during a conversation. Better Slack conversation context: @GitHub can use shared Slack messages and threads as context, making it easier to reference discussions without copying and pasting details. Improved reliability: We’ve made several improvements to reduce errors, improve task startup, and help @GitHub recover more smoothly from interruptions in Slack and Teams. Join the discussion within the GitHub Community. The post Multi-repository support and other improvements for GitHub in Slack and Teams appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub's Slack and Teams agent can now create issues and PRs across multiple repositories. This is a moderate workflow convenience for teams using Copilot.

items.title: Xcode 27 runner image generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now use the generally available Xcode 27 runner image to build and test your Apple applications in GitHub Actions. Previously in public preview, this GitHub-hosted image runs on macOS 27 and includes the Xcode 27 toolchain and Apple SDKs. Xcode-based images Each image supports one major Xcode version rather than targeting a specific operating system version. This makes it easier to select the toolchain your project needs and know what each runner provides. Get started To use the image, set your workflow’s runs-on: value to one of these labels: xcode-27 xcode-27-xlarge If you already use these labels, you don’t need to change your workflows. The image is available on Apple Silicon (arm64) runners only, not Intel runners. To view the installed software or report an issue, visit the runner-images repository. The post Xcode 27 runner image generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Xcode 27 runners are now GA in GitHub Actions. This is relevant only for iOS client work, which is outside First Mate's core web stack.

items.title: Open source license compliance generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Enterprises can now manage their dependencies’ licenses at scale with sophisticated, ruleset-based checks that enforce a centralized policy. Open source license compliance is now generally available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GHEC, for repositories with GitHub Code Security enabled. How it works Open source license compliance expands on the capabilities of the dependency review action by introducing an enterprise-wide license policy. The policy is activated by targeting repositories with a ruleset that uses a new Require license compliance results before merging condition, similar to the existing code scanning conditions. When developers open pull requests that add or modify dependencies, license checks automatically ensure each new or changed dependency has an acceptable license. The feature annotates the pull request with a message about each noncompliant dependencies. These annotations must be addressed by removing or replacing the dependency, amending the license policy, or creating package exceptions. Open source license compliance introduces a new predefined enterprise role, Enterprise Open-Source License Manager. Assign this role to individuals or teams who should review and approve closure requests. Policy managers receive email notifications about pending requests and can review them from the enterprise console. What’s new and improved Since the public preview release in June, we’ve made several improvements: License information is now available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud data residency customers. This not only enables the license compliance feature, but also populates the dependency graph and Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) exports with license data. License policy changes now emit audit log events, for integration with external systems of record. There are new API endpoints for downloading, updating, and replacing the enterprise license policy. items.title: LaTeX renderer
items.excerpt: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office, which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well: We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool Here's an example link. The tool uses Pako 2.1.0, MathJax 4.1.3, faster-latex 0.3.1, and DOMPurify 3.4.16. Tags: latex, paul-ford, tools, urls, ai, generative-ai, llms
items.why_it_matters: Small Simon Willison tool built with Claude. It shows llms.txt guiding agents to build URL-encoded documents, an interesting agent-readable pattern but of minor practical impact.

items.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
items.excerpt: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang, How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic, claude, ai, claude-code, llms, addy-osmani, coding-agents, generative-ai, agentic-engineering, code-review
items.why_it_matters: Claude Code team describes review as continuous, with Claude reviewing changes before humans. This maps directly onto our gated review pipelines and our verification-over-vibes practice.

items.title: My AI Dark Factory Dream Is Dead (Here's What Actually Works)
items.author: Cole Medin
items.excerpt: The dark factory sounds like the dream: hand your agents a massive app and they ship it straight to production. I spent a big part of this year building one, and even with AGI it wouldn't work. Because as cheesy as it sounds, LLMs can't read our minds. So I turned it into an AI software factory, and honestly I'm not actually giving up that much autonomy! I plan each release up front, the factory rips through the issues in parallel, and I test it all in staging before it ships. Here's the whole process and the lessons I learned getting here! ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ - Port, the platform for running your own AI Software Factory (free for up to 15 seats): https://hubs.la/Q04xSGt70 Thanks to Port for backing this video! ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ - Join Dynamous for the new Agentic Coding Course 2.0 - the core of the course is now COMPLETE: https://dynamous.ai - The AI Software Factory (open source): https://github.com/coleam00/ai-software-factory Dan Shapiro, The Five Levels (where the dark factory comes from): https://www.danshapiro.com/blog/2026/01/the-five-levels-from-spicy-autocomplete-to-the-software-factory/ Dex Horthy, Why Software Factories Fail: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ib5GBkD555M ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 0:00 The Dark Factory Dream 1:50 Why the Dark Factory Doesn't Work 3:31 Agents Can't Read Your Mind 4:24 Who Maintains the Codebase 5:04 The Software Factory I Run Now 5:47 Plan the Scope, Not the Whole App 7:34 Port (Sponsor) 9:03 Part 1: Plan and Split the Release 10:51 Holdout Scenarios 11:48 Dependencies and Human in the Loop 13:32 Part 2: The Core Loop 14:26 Validation vs Code Review 15:32 The Manager Agent 16:35 Files the Factory Can Never Edit 17:02 Mixing Models to Save Tokens 17:40 Part 3: Test It in Staging 18:39 Final Thoughts ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Join me as I push the limits of what is possible with AI. I'll be uploading videos weekly - at least every Wednesday at 7:00 PM CDT!
items.why_it_matters: Practical lessons on parallel agent pipelines: plan releases up front, run issues in parallel, verify in staging. This matches First Mate's plan-first, verification-over-vibes approach.
